transcript:
Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Red Eye.
I'm your host, Edipalmian and with me in the studio is my friend and colleague, Niklas Savos.
Today we are excited to speak to Asif Suria, an entrepreneur and investor in the US,
focusing on a specific investing strategy that we haven't talked that much about in the podcast yet.
So Niklas, which book will we discuss?
So the title for this conversation is Asif's book, The Event Driven Edge,
in Investing, in which he explains six different event driven strategies,
for example, merger arbitrage and stock buybacks.
And what do you think about the book?
So I like how the author has structured the book between presenting the evidence
for why the different strategies work and how investors can use them.
And as with many things in Investing, there is a lot of noise
and the author helps us to distill which events carry more weight in the six strategies.
And we think this book is useful both for focused, special situations, investors,
but also for long term investors in general.
The event driven Edge in Investing was published by Harman House in 2024
and we are delighted to discuss it on the show today.
Here comes our conversation with Asif Suria.
Hello Asif and welcome to Investing by the book's podcast.
Thank you so much for having me on today.
I'm very excited to be on.
It's great to have you and where are we reaching you today?
I'm based on the San Francisco Bay Area, just a little bit south of the city of San Francisco.
And to begin, we are curious to hear about your background
and when your passion for investing started.
Yes, so my passion for investing started in 2001.
So this was right after the dot com bubble at first and we were in a deep bear market.
Now probably not the best time to start investing but it was a great learning experience
because I thought how could the market go any lower than it already had
and sure enough it does always.
So that is a great way to start learning.
I started out as a value investor and then over time,
especially during the great recession or 2008-2009,
I started looking into event driven situations starting with my job at Raj.
On the professional side, I was a technologist and worked in technology,
including enterprise software for almost 20 years.
And my last job before I started focusing full time on inside our
job at Raj was with the mental health care company in San Francisco.
And today we will speak about your book, the event driven edge in investing.
How did it come about?
Yeah, it was a very certain bit in some sense.
I met a friend for lunch in 2023.
He had recently retired after working at Google.
And we were both discussing things that were on our bucket list.
So one of the things on his bucket list was to go to the Berkshire Hathaway meeting.
And I realized that that was on my list as well.
And so I decided to join him for the Berkshire Hathaway meeting.
And that caught me thinking about what are the other things on my bucket list?
And one of them was to write a book.
I started writing a book almost eight or nine years ago.
And I figured it was time to share my investing experience,
all the different case studies that encountered as an event driven investor.
So I reached out to Vitaly Katsinelsen and I reached out to Tobias.
Carl Lyle and both of them did warm introductions with Hyramin House.
Actually within one hour of each other.
So I was able to get Hyramin House on a Zoom call.
And I told them, you know, it's been 25 years since dual Greenblatt's book.
You can be a stock market genius came out.
And maybe it's time for a fresh look at event driven strategies or special situations.
And it looks like that resonated with them.
And that's how the book came about.
And for those not familiar with the event driven investing or so-called special situations.
How would you describe it?
Yeah, so there are certain kind of events that have a significant impact on the price of a company stock.
Quarterly earnings announcements.
One of those things that everybody is familiar with.
But there are other kind of corporate events, right?
Like one company buying another company.
A company deciding to break itself up into two or more parts.
Or even a company declaring bankruptcy.
So each of these events, whether it's M&A, whether it's spin-offs, or that's bankruptcies,
they lead to opportunities for investors that they can benefit from.
So investing based on these kinds of corporate events is called event driven investing.
Or more popularly special situations invested.
And I mean, as you said before, you tilted to become an invent driven investor yourself.
What do you think the advantages are of that strategy?
Yeah, so if you look at most stock markets these days, they're very efficient.
As soon as something happens, such as Trump winning the US elections,
that information starts being accommodated, assimilated into the market very quickly in the short term at least.
Then there are sentiments of fear and greed that can move entire markets well outside where they should be trading.
So sometimes they trade well above where the intrinsic value should be.
Sometimes they trade well below.
So that is one kind of macro level inefficiency that patient investors could benefit from.
The old saying buy when there's blood on the streets and be fearful when you're greedy.
But that doesn't happen all the time.
So event driven investing in a similar way creates some inefficiencies or provide signals that may not be very well understood by the market right away.
And that's what creates the opportunities for investors that understand these inefficiencies or these signals.
And what do you think are the biggest risk in this strategy?
Absolutely, so there is risk in every strategy.
No matter how exciting it sounds.
And there's a season for every strategy.
So for example, merger arbitrage, which is a strategy where you buy a company after an acquisition is announced and wait for the deal to close.
That used to work really well about three or four years ago when interest rates were near zero.
And the regularity environment in the US was not as restrictive as it is now.
This could obviously change now if there's a new Trump administration and they make some changes on the regulatory side of things.
So much arbitrage was great three or four years ago.
Not so good this year.
But at the same time, if you look at something like spin-offs, they were not working so well about three or four years ago.
They've started working much better now.
So that's one of the risks where you can understand why your certain strategy might be good for the current environment and why it might not always work.
And that's the reason I track six different strategies.
So there's constant idea generation, even if first strategy is not in season.
And when you say that strategy is not in season, is that sort of, I mean, usually in investing, it takes a few years for you to understand that the strategy don't work.
And then you've already made a lot of decisions. So I mean, how do you sort of evolve continuously with that?
Well, I mean, when you look at, you have to look at every different aspect of what's happening, right?
So you've got to look at what's happening with interest rates.
So when interest rates are high, people have other alternatives.
They can put their money in treasuries and earn a decent return.
They can put their money in CDs and so on and so forth.
So much arbitrage becomes less attractive in that environment.
It also becomes less attractive because you expect a greater rate of return from it.
And usually you would get that only in the risky deals.
So you have to look at what's happening in the macro environment.
On the spin off side, you also have to understand what's going on with general market valuations and so on and so forth.
Our companies in trouble are trying to spin off because they're trying to get rid of a bad division.
Are they trying to spin off because things are going really well and they just want to allow the spin off to be its own independent company and grow.
So you have to look at things in that context.
There's also insider transactions where I've seen at times that during the COVID pandemic, the March 2020 big drop in the market inside a stepped in and started buying way more than I'd ever seen them buy in the 10 years prior.
So you can see these signals happen in some some sense in real time.
And you can adjust with strategies you want to focus all based on that.
And as you mentioned in in your book, you describe six different events strategies in detail.
But we're curious how you selected these six.
Yeah, so there are strategies like bankruptcies that are so complex that very few retail or even professional investors can participate in them.
I selected six strategies for the book based on the ones that are already accessible for all investors and not just institutional or professional investors.
And I personally use most of these strategies for more than a decade and I cover them on my website inside of a charge.
And if you go deeper in a few of the strategies and starting with insider transactions, you mentioned that some transactions by insiders are more or less noise while others can be seen as a strong catalyst.
Could you provide an example from from the book that shows the difference?
Yeah, so I mostly focus on insider buying and opportunistic inside of buying.
So by opportunistic buying, I mean an insider that is not buying based on a pre established buying plan that they follow the SEC.
And someone who hasn't purchased stock frequently in the past.
So I look for those kind of insiders to provide signals.
One good example that I discussed as a case study in the book was insider buying in a company called vertex pharmaceuticals.
This is a company that is quite large right now and they had a very successful cystic fibrosis franchise.
And there was an independent director who bought some stock in November 2020.
And every weekend I write about insider purchases.
And one of my subscribers read about this insider purchase and he wrote to be saying, oh, this is two briefcase Bruce that's buying the stock.
And if two briefcase Bruce is buying, I'm going to buy as well.
And I wasn't sure what he was talking about. So I reached out to him and I said, hey, what do you mean this is two briefcase Bruce, who's two briefcase Bruce.
So he told me that in the early 1990s, two briefcase Bruce and him used to work in the same company together.
Two briefcase Bruce was actually Bruce sacks.
And he had an excellent work ethic where he would work throughout the week.
And then on the weekend, when this was back at a time where you couldn't take your laptop home with you.
He would fill two briefcase is full of work related documents and take them home and work on them over the weekend and come back on Monday.
So he had a reputation for both being brilliant as well as being very hard working.
And so I took a closer look at this and I realized that he's been on the board of the directors of the company for almost 10 years.
But he never bought stock in the company before.
And then in August 2021, both him and the CEO of buying stock, I decided to make an exception.
I normally don't invest in biotech companies because I don't understand them.
But if two briefcase Bruce was buying, I thought it would make sense to buy as well.
The financials of the company were actually pretty good. So they were making good money.
This wasn't a preclinical biotech. This was a company that was actually making good money and was growing.
This was a decision a little bit easier.
This is a historical example.
You know, this is something I wrote about in the book and you know, I wrote the book almost well over a year ago at this point.
A more recent example is the hotel reed.
Pebblebrook hotel trust.
So the CEO has a long history with the company and he started buying in August.
So there's a couple of months ago.
A hotel reed that had cut its dividend as you would expect during COVID.
But when the business rebounded after the pandemic, instead of increasing the dividend again, they kept the dividend really small and invested the rest of the money in refurbishing their properties and fixing the properties.
They also refocused from business to desired travel.
So given how well the company is doing, I think they are going to increase the dividend now that their capital expenditure cycle is winding down.
So to make things interesting, the street also trades well below the value of all the hotels it holds.
So here's something it hasn't played out yet, but I think he's getting ready to increase the dividend.
Now that the capital cycle is over and you get a hotel property that's trading below its value on the books.
And just to ask, I mean, how big was that transaction?
Because I think one of the points you make is that sort of big and the infrequent transactions carry more signals than others.
Yeah, so in some sense, I do look for big transactions.
In this case, I don't think it was a very large transaction, but I think he might make a few more before things turn around.
So it is more the infrequency of the transaction where somebody hasn't bought for a really long time and then suddenly they buy.
And you know, you hope that it actually makes sense, but the more likely scenarios it might not make sense based on all the data you have in front of you.
And after a very long time following this, I'm beginning to realize that when it doesn't make sense as well, it's actually more interesting.
Yeah, because it's interesting to know, I mean, you see the signal and you seem to very be very good at picking those up.
But then the question is when should you actually make the decision to buy or sell something.
And in the book, you write that quote, insiders like value investors are often early to the party.
So why do you believe this is the case?
So markets are often irrational, right? They never trade at where the intrinsic value of a company should be.
And so insiders like value investors are viewing things rationally.
So what they are seeing can often take weeks or months to play out and the price action might even take even longer after the situation has played out.
So I often find that value investors and insiders, they see value, but they early because the market has been continue to remain irrational for a little bit longer.
So I've seen this pattern over and over again, where whether it's J Hogue Buying Zillow a few months before they announced a new CEO or in this case, a CEO of Pebble Brook Buying.
Often it can be several weeks or months in advance.
Even in the case of Bruce Axis, first purchase was in November, 2020.
And the stock really actually took off after a second purchase in August, 2021.
So it can take some time for these situations to play out.
And do you usually wait or how do you handle that situation?
That's a tough question.
If the company makes a lot of sense to me right away, I do end up buying.
Sometimes when I might actually have it on a watch list for a long time.
So I maintain a very long watch list.
Some that are based on inside of transactions.
Some that are based on meeting other investors at a bookshadowing meeting.
And I got some ideas there.
This month in November in our November newsletter actually took an idea that I added on the watch list three years ago.
Because now I'm starting to see really good inflection in the stock price.
So at the end of the day, it really is an idea generation strategy for me.
And then the inflection or when it becomes interesting could be several weeks, months,
or maybe even several years later.
And in the book and also in this conversation, you mentioned that you do work every weekend.
And something that you mentioned in the book is that you every weekend calculate a sell by ratio.
So what is this?
Yeah, I probably work more on the weekends that will work due to the week.
I've joking.
But every weekend, we look at every single insider transaction every purchase and every sale.
We clean the data.
And then we calculate the aggregate amount of insider buying and aggregate amount of insider selling.
And we divide the insider selling by the insider buying to create something called the sell by ratio.
And the reason we do this is we want to track this to see our insider selling significantly more stock than they used to or inside us buying all of a sudden a whole lot more stock than they used to.
You have what is called earnings related quiet periods.
So you know few weeks before earnings are released and few weeks even a few days after you're not going to see a lot of insider transactions.
So outside of that, once you adjust for that, if you suddenly see a big spike and inside a buying insider selling that can be a macro signal.
So for me, a macro signal of sorts was in March 2020 when inside a buying exceeded inside the selling for the first time in a decade.
I'd never seen them before week after week inside a selling was almost 20 or 30 times the amount of insider buying.
But in that one instance for two weeks inside a buying exceeded insider selling and you could also see this at the sector level.
So in mid 2020 when WTI crude futures when negative oil prices were negative energy company inside us really stepped in and started buying handover first.
I saw the same thing last year in early 2023 after Silicon Valley bank failed.
You could see that the bank insiders were coming out of the woodwork to buy.
So I love looking at aggregate inside a buying and selling data both to see if it's giving me a macro signal on the whole market or if it's telling me something about a specific sector.
And throughout the book you describe how investors can benefit from when some of the six strategies work in tandem such as buybacks together with insider buying.
Can you mention a situation for us where where this situation made you interested?
Yeah, one of these interesting situation was the acquisition of this biotic company called biohaven by Pfizer.
So the acquisition price was around 148 dollars biohaven was trading around 141 when I wrote about it.
So you got a chance to make about $78 on the acquisition and then right before the acquisition happened I noticed that an insider direct of the company was buying stock.
This is highly unusual. You don't see somebody buying stock, especially an insider right before a deal is supposed to close.
And the spread on the deal was something like 50 cents and that made no sense.
Why would a direct of the company want to buy this clock for 50 cents a profit.
And so I took a very close look at it and they had a situation where Pfizer was going to spin off certain assets.
So they were interested in the main migraine related drugs that biohaven made and everything else was going to get spun out after the merger closed into another company which they also decided to call biohaven just to confuse us investors.
So I think his interest was in the new biohaven because he knew that by buying stock before the merger closed he would get the spin off shares.
And this was a strange situation where Pfizer actually put several hundred million dollars into the spin off as well.
So you had a spread you could capture on the merger.
You got the spin off and you notice that that was inside a buying going on.
Sure enough the spin off went on to do very well and we continue to see inside a buying in the biohaven for months and years after the spin off as well.
And just to recap a bit on the strategy as a whole I mean in merger arbitrage situations there is of course like a high probability that the merger closes but there is a risk also that it's not and then you usually have quite a big sell off.
So talking about risks in general how do you how do you think about portfolio construction in connection with an event driven strategy.
Yeah so you're absolutely right none of these strategies are risk we as especially merger arbitrage is also called risk arbitrage because you are taking on the risk that the deal might not close.
And so with a risk arbitrage the way I used to position things realizing that 95% of all act mergers and acquisitions actually close.
The way I used to position things was I would do my standard position size like 5% of the portfolio.
And if I felt like you know I had high confidence in the deal closing that I might go even more I used to do 10% back when regulatory environment wasn't so bad.
Given how difficult it is these days to get a deal through regulators I don't no longer do that I'm back to my standard position size of 5%.
In case of highly risky deals I might even go down to a 2% position so I might scale back the position size based on the amount of risk I perceive in the deal.
In some situations I might actually use options I might use call options to limit my exposure and to use the returns a little bit or I might even buy put options as protection.
And some merge arbitrage focus investors will use a multi-leg option strategy to both control risk and increase the potential returns.
And how do you handle the emotional aspects of things I mean usually when you have sort of a date that you're waiting for and you know that the risk a risk that there is a risk that something could happen in a negative sense I mean have you have you learned to cope with that or is that still an issue for you.
I think it's always going to be an issue for investors right I try to control for that quite a bit through the position sizing so if I if I had one third of my portfolio in a risky position that wasn't working out I think I'll have trouble sleeping at night and so by using position sizing I think I control for that quite a bit.
I'm usually not in just one merge arbitrage situation I might be in multiple situations at the same time and then I have a portfolio constructed from other ideas as well so merge arbitrage plays a certain role in the portfolio and again within the specific ones I'm investing I'm using position size so that it doesn't blow up the entire portfolio for deal blows up.
You can also focus on deals that you know don't have the widest spread and attract the largest attention so everybody was interested in Elon Musk buying Twitter because I was a widespread on that it worked out well people are interested in Microsoft buying activation blizzard that worked out well.
But then jet blue acquisition of spirit allies did not work out well.
Paper Street acquisition of capri is not going so well right now so you know you have to look at these situations and say am I participating in the riskiest mergers with the biggest potential profit or am I participating in lures mergers where I can sleep at night if I use proper position sizing.
And just to get everything right here so in terms of portfolio construction you think differently in all these different six event driven strategies yeah right.
Absolutely so if it's an idea where I've done fundamental work based on a spin off or an insider transaction it's a 5% position.
If it's a merge arbitrage situation then it's the risk that determines if I'll make it a 10% position or maybe a 2% position.
Great so let's move over to another type of strategy which is spin-offs which we have seen quite quite a lot actually in Sweden in the last years.
And of course a lot has been written about the outperformance of spin-offs and you present the evidence for why these situations may work and one reason is forced selling as some institutions are not allowed to own stocks in a spin off due to for example size constraints.
And another more long term benefit that you mentioned is that the company gets less bureaucracy and starting with the first reason can you please talk about when the aspect of size can have a particularly large impact.
Yeah so let's say you own a large company like Jeffries which was an investment bank but it also because of its merger with Lucadia had a bunch of operating businesses.
And so if you were a portfolio manager that had mostly focused on financial firms and you had Jeffries and a Jeffries spun off energy company like witness energy.
So you not only have the size mismatch where you end up with a company that's only a few hundred million dollars in market cap but also a company in the energy industry which is cyclical and maybe it's something that you normally avoid.
So you have a situation where this force selling by professional investors because of size mismatch because it's an industry they don't follow, they don't understand or they avoid.
So that's one of the reasons you could end up with opportunities because of the force selling.
And why do you think because we have seen this many times why don't the sort of the forced sellers why don't they sell before because usually it's sort of mentioned that the spin off is going to happen so why don't they sell before the spin off is actually done.
Actually that's a really good question because sometimes after the spin off the parent can be even more attractive.
So maybe they're like Jeffries and they say investment banking is a wonderful business in certain market conditions with really good margins compared to a cyclical business like oil and gas.
And so they might look at it and say I'm actually glad they're getting rid of this division that was dragging down the parent company.
And if anything they might buy more after the spin off and I've personally done that where I've looked at a company doing a spin off.
And I either buy before the spin off because I like both the parent and the spin off post spin off which is what is happening with Western digital right now.
Or I might buy after the spin off and I say they got rid of the bad company if you will they loaded it up with debt and the parent is more attractive.
And I think an interesting point you bring up is the timing aspect here that about when to buy a spin off and I mean taking those two aspects I mentioned into account for selling should be completed, completed quite quickly.
So I mean how do you keep up to date with the with the status and how long how long does it typically take.
So we keep a list of all spin off situations just like we keep a list of all M&A merger arbitrage situations in the US.
But I personally don't look at you know what kind of trading volume has happened in the spin off post spin off for me spin off investing is more opportunistic.
So I'll usually look at them because something about the parent of the spin off got my attention because a subscriber asked me about it somebody who told me about you know to briefcase Bruce might mention he asked about you think of Western digital.
Or there might be an event like an insider transaction in the parent before the spin off that make make me take a look.
So that's how I do it is very opportunistic.
But my friend Rich how focuses only on spin offs he very carefully looks at you know what kind of trading volume are you seeing post spin off.
And is it going to be like a week or is it going to be three months before most of the force selling is done.
So he takes a he does the qualitative work and it does the more quantitative work of figuring out when all the trading has happened that's not usually how I approach it.
Interesting and the the benefit of less bureaucracy for the company I mean it's quite appealing for the long term trajectory of a business.
Do you have an example for us where with this change was especially clear.
Oh absolutely there's so many examples going maybe almost two decades back you had Chipotle the Mexican restaurant chain that was spun out of McDonald's.
It was able to super charge its growth by opening a whole lot more locations so that did very well you had Ferrari that got spun out of Fiat Chrysler.
So that help Ferrari continue to perform very well on its own not be under a large bureaucratic automobile company.
We spoke about witness energy which has done very well once it came out of an investment bank Jeffries.
So you have so many of the situations where you can see that if the company that is being spun out is good they're not loading it up with a lot of debt.
Freeing them up out of the parent company really super charges growth.
And we're not going to mention all strategies from from your book in this episode.
We encourage everyone to buy it and read it for themselves but the one that I would like to bring up is management changes as you mentioned as a strategy.
And I'd rather we also put a lot of effort and focus on evaluating the people our business.
We think this is very important but why do you consider management changes an event driven investing strategy.
Yeah so I feel like the CEO of a firm they define the direction of the form and more importantly the capital allocation strategy.
So if you look at a CEO and you see that you know their pay structure is egregious.
It's very high and they're not aligned with shareholders that can mean something very significant in negative for a portfolio company if you already own it.
Or if you see that the CEO is thinking about on stakeholders like employees and shareholders.
And you know their pay structures aligned with the interests of shareholders.
They can do very well for the company.
Or you can also look at their past performance like we did with Larry cult who came out or done her and he did very well a GE.
So you can look at the past performance at a different company and see if they really move the needle.
If they skate there for a long enough time to make a change happen.
So I see management changes is a very critical thing that strangely enough not a lot of investors pay a lot of attention to.
And so I consider that a very significant event and I added it as an event when strategy of the book.
Something that is quite challenging I think as an investor is these kind of transition periods that can happen in companies when you had a long standing CEO that is leaving and then the company hasn't announced the new CEO.
How do you deal with such situations?
Yeah, this is a difficult situation. I don't have a specific strategy for it.
I would look at it and see if the underlying business is very strong.
And if there are any red flags caused by this departure.
So is it a sudden departure where there wasn't enough transition time provided to the board.
Or was this a long transition period where you know you have almost a year or longer to make sure that somebody else is coming in and it's going to be successful as a CEO.
So strength of business and the transition period or something that I'm interested in that I look at.
Otherwise, I'm not quite as concerned.
It also kind of depends on a case by case basis.
So if you look at somebody like fill light, found out of Nike, how would shoes at Starbucks Larry culprit now a GE or Bob I got a Disney, if one of these were leaving, then I would be concerned and I might even consider selling.
But if it is not one of these superstars CEO's and the business is strong, there's a long transition time, then I'm a little less concerned.
Good point because I think quite many of the investors that we speak to and quite many of our listeners of this podcast are like a long term investors are looking for companies to hold for many years in cases.
Do you think they can also benefit from taking part of these kind of strategies that you are outlining in the book?
Absolutely. Like I said, my primary goal with these strategies and even with the book is to help you find strategies that generate ideas at the end of the day.
You have to do your own work on them. You have to understand the companies and then buy them and hopefully hold them for the long term.
When I bought vertex pharmaceuticals, it's been three years since I did that. I still have that stock with me. I hope to hold for another few years.
So these are long term ideas that these strategies end up generating for me.
The other advantage of doing your own work and fully understanding these companies or as much as you can understand given public information is when something doesn't work out and the market drops.
It gives you the conviction to hold on to the company even when things don't appear to be going well with the overall market.
So doing your own work and diligence actually gives you the confidence to hold on if something is not going right.
And if you've done your work and if something is not going right with the company, you will also understand that it's a company-specific issue and not a market-specific issue.
I think it's interesting with these kind of combinations as well. I mean, we talked a little bit about it before but is there any other combination of these kind of strategies that you outlined in the book or other event driven strategies that you would like to highlight that you have found are more powerful.
Now the combination is the ones that I find the most fascinating. They don't happen very often.
But we ended up building some custom screens on inside arbitrage so that we know when they happen.
So one of them is we call it a spin-sider screen. It's spin-offs with inside a buying. So we run that screen to take a look at you know which spin-offs are seen inside a buy and which ones.
The buying is happening in the parent versus the actual spin-off. We also have what is called a double-dipper custom screen.
